Reading passages — read first (Q1–10)

Passage A — Unit 12: Nail Art

The art of painting pictures on people's fingernails has a rich history dating back over 2,500 years in Asia. Today, this ancient tradition remains popular in nail salons globally. While many clients select simple solid colors, others choose intricate nail art to make their nails stand out. Skilled nail artists utilize specialized miniature tools, stickers, and decorative jewels to paint detailed patterns. They often work for 20 minutes or longer per nail, charging $15 to $30 for each nail. Although custom nail art is a lucrative commercial business, American painter Rick Mazzaferro creates nail designs purely as a non-profit hobby. He paints miniature landscapes—including deer near rivers, snowy mountain sunsets, and the Golden Gate Bridge—on his friends' nails, using fingernails as a unique canvas to express artistic creativity.

Passage B — Unit 13: New Homes for Animals

Across the globe, numerous wild animal species face severe habitat loss caused by human industrial development and natural disasters. When habitats are ruined, affected wildlife species risk dying out or becoming extinct. To counter this threat, wildlife conservationists formulate strategic relocation plans. They analyze animal migration habits, dietary requirements, social behaviors, and potential diseases. Conservationists then relocate endangered populations to safe, ecologically balanced sanctuaries. A notable example is the international strategy to transfer wild tigers from India to protected areas in Cambodia. Relocating threatened species and establishing secure habitats is crucial for maintaining ecological health and biodiversity worldwide.
